issues.title: Discuss tradeoff between replay resistance and efficiency
issues.author: jhoyla
issues.body:
When loading a single website it's not uncommon to have dozens, if not hundreds, of requests to the same FQDN. Creating and verifying dozens of signed requests that only differ in the nonce almost simultaneously would be very inefficient, but not requiring a nonce (and thus allowing the signature to be cached) allows for replays. Perhaps the draft should discuss options for balancing these two.
Some options include:
1. Allow small numbers of replays. This probably requires state on the server side, but given that we need to store nonces to enforce them this might not be too bad.
2. Allow replays but only for signatures with very short (e.g. 5 second) lifetimes. This still lets a malicious client do less work than the server (unless the server caches the verification result I guess), but given that this is non-repudiatable, I don't think it's a significant risk. 
3. Enforcing nonces strictly, but providing a cookie along with each response to a signed request. The client can send a few signed requests in parallel, and once the first one has a response switch to using the cookie. The downside of this is that if an adversary gets a signed request they can exchange it for a cookie, which can then be replayed, but this can be managed through cookie mechanisms.

comments.author: thibmeu
comments.body:

comments.body:

comments.author: jhoyla
comments.body:
So HTTP Message Sigs is similar to DBSC in some ways, but I think the trade-offs are very different. First, DBSC is aimed at human users, so things like adding a roundtrip have a much higher weight than they do for bots. Second, HMS cares much less about sessions. Whereas a user might want to stay logged in for days or weeks, a bot is more likely to have a short lived interaction with a zone. It also may be using the same signing key whilst acting on behalf of multiple different users, so I think the session paradigm doesn't really apply neatly. Third, we don't really care about the bots activities being linkable to each other, except in so far as they link together the activities of a single user.

The core concerns raised by MT seem to be about efficiency vs security, which also apply here, but I think the answers are very different. We rely on the security of the signature generator more, because we're talking corporate IT, rather than end-user devices. 

With respect to your first comment, I am worried that most people will in practice implement option 0, allow unbounded numbers of replays, and only request new signatures on suspicion of abuse. In the unbounded replay scenario the scheme is relatively efficient for both parties, at the expense of security. Adding text describing the trade-off between efficiency and security and different patterns one might employ will hopefully steer people away from option 0.

issues.title: Threat model: Multi-CDN
issues.author: jhoyla
issues.body:
In a multi-CDN use-case all the CDNs need to trust each other, because one CDN can use signed requests that it receives to impersonate an agent to the others. This attack exists even if the CDN uses `Accept-Signature` to provide a fresh nonce, because the malicious CDN can simply forward the `Accept-Signature` message to the agent.  We should add a sentence to the threat model covering this possibility.

I'm not sure how this can be avoided without cooperation from the client, because even if the CDN creates a structured / authenticated nonce, if the client doesn't understand the structure it will sign it even if it comes from the "wrong" CDN. Even with cooperation from the client, I'm not sure how the client could easily / reliably distinguish between CDNs.

comments.author: thibmeu
comments.body:
Possibly along this line, enhancing the security considerations to mention HTTP Message Signatures would be one identification method, and is going to be used in conjunction with others (old like IP ranges, new like req mTLS).

If the IP range of the origin was allowlisted, that would already reduce potential abuse, even if this is out of scope for this draft.

issues.title: Performance of a global nonce store
issues.author: jhoyla
issues.body: To enforce nonces strictly the origin needs to keep a list of all nonces that it has seen whose signatures are still valid. For a multi-server architecture this could amount to a sync on a global database, which could have a significant performance cost, especially as most requests will both read and write. In practice it might make more sense to enforce weaker guarantees in the name of performance.

comments.author: thibmeu
comments.body:
Agree. I think it should suffice for the draft to remove the MUST on verify nonce uniqueness to MAY to solve the issue.

A specific addition in the security consideration can be added as well

issues.title: Support for CBOR and COSE Keys
issues.author: thibmeu
issues.body:
There are multiple places where CBOR and CBOR Web keys could be introduced.

1. HTTP Message Signature directory format. I'd be in favor of add `+json` at the end of the directory Media type, so that we can declare `+cbor` when relevant
2. JSON Web Thumbprint is used as a key id. This is great because it provides a unique key id that is derived from the key material. I'd be in favor of sticking to ONE key id derivation method, even though [RFC 9679](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9679.html) defines a Thumbprint for COSE Keys.

issues.title: Consider negative test vectors
issues.author: thibmeu
issues.body:
This relates to https://github.com/cloudflareresearch/web-bot-auth/issues/4

It should be fine to limit these vectors to Ed25519 initially.

comments.author: AVAVERIFY
comments.body:
Support for doing this, and for the shape proposed on the list: one fault per vector, with the request, the expected outcome, and the expected reason, against the B.1.4 key.

Second implementer datapoint on the structure. Our merchant-side verifier ships a typed reason vocabulary in production, currently 35 names, and every reason carries a conclusive flag: whether the check completed and failed, or could not complete. That is the 19/17 split from ParallaxGrain's message and Appendix C.1's invalid and unverified one level down, arrived at independently. Two implementations converging on the same two-layer structure from opposite sides of the fence suggests the structure is the part worth standardizing: outcome from C.1, then a named reason beneath it. The names can be argued; the layering has held up under production traffic on one side and the autonomous-agent experiment on the other.

Two guardrails from the merchant seat worth building into the vector schema. First, the boundary between the layers is load-bearing: a reason that means the verifier could not decide must never appear under an invalid outcome, because downstream software switches on the outcome and will treat the pair as a rejection. Our schema enforces that pairing, and the vector schema should too, so no vector can state an incoherent outcome and reason combination. Second, the vectors should define what a verifier concludes and stay silent on what it discloses. Named reasons to a legitimate operator are exactly the debugging value the agent datapoint shows; the same names returned unconditionally are a probing oracle for a forger. Conclude versus disclose is a policy line each deployment draws, and the vector set should not draw it for them.

Our reason names and their conclusive flags are public in the verifier source (github.com/AVA-PAY/ava-pay, src/verifier). Happy to contribute them as input alongside the 36 when the set is drafted, and to wire the resulting vectors into our suite the way we did E.2.3, so the set ships tested against at least two independent implementations from day one.

comments.author: ParallaxGrain
comments.body:
Here's the set: https://github.com/ParallaxGrain/webbotauth-negative-vectors

17 vectors, one fault per vector, on the B.1.4 key from RFC 9421 since the draft already uses it. Each one gives the request, the outcome it should get from Appendix C.1, and a suggested reason underneath. If the reason vocabulary isn't useful to you, check the outcome and ignore the rest.

COVERAGE.md goes through all 37 failures my verifier can report and says what became of each: 17 are vectors, 20 are not. The count quoted earlier in this thread is out of date. Building the vectors settled two classifications against the text and turned up one condition that had no name yet, so it is 37 now, split 19/18.

One thing I could not write a vector for. Section 5.2 makes tag="web-bot-auth" a MUST for signers, RFC 9421 3.2.1 says verification MUST fail when an application's own requirements are not met, and 5.4 says the Origin MAY discard a foreign tag instead. Those are two different answers to the same request, and one of them is not an outcome Appendix C.1 defines, so I had nothing to put in the expected field. Written up in COVERAGE.md.

@AVAVERIFY I did both the things you suggested. Outcome and reason are checked against each other twice, and the generator won't write a vector where the two disagree. Conclude vs disclose has its own section, with your comment linked.

Issues and PRs welcome, especially if a vector expects the wrong reason.

comments.author: AVAVERIFY
comments.body:
Results from running the 17 against our production verifier, as promised. The short version: 15 of 17 outcomes agree, and the two that do not are one sentence in Appendix C.1 rather than a defect on either side. The longer version has a part I owe you plainly.

Three of your vectors found real bugs in our verifier, and two of them were verify-through holes. NV-19: we never checked for repeated component identifiers, built a signature base with @authority twice, and verified a signature over it, which RFC 9421 Section 2.5 forbids outright. NV-13: given several Signature-Agent members and none label-matched, we attributed by header order, which means a request could name a reputable origin first and its own second and we would have attributed to the first, exactly the Section 5.2.2 MUST NOT. NV-17: a directory-type member carrying a path, which Section 5.5 says to ignore; we took the origin, discarded the path, and reported our strongest binding claim for it. Before your set we agreed on 13 of 17; all three are fixed with regression tests and deployed, and the fix for NV-17 is the same one your README discloses for your own verifier. Your set did in an afternoon what our own suite had not done in two months, and I would say that on the record even if it were more comfortable not to.

The two remaining disagreements, NV-12 and post-fix NV-17, are the same question, and it is the one your Open section already names. You read C.1's "unverified" as "discovery could not run"; we read it as "a check we ran could not complete." A signed request with no Signature-Agent, or with a sole member the text says to ignore, is definitively non-conforming to a MUST, and we know it without fetching anything, so we say invalid. You say unverified because nothing was checked. Notably you classify those two cells differently from each other on your side and call both defensible, so this is one unresolved word producing three different splits across two implementations. That is a text problem for the group to settle, and the vectors are what surfaced it.

On granularity, a concession: eleven of your seventeen conditions arrive at a merchant from our verifier as a single name, malformed_signature_header, and in three of those the header is not malformed at all. Your fix texts for NV-07 and NV-05 are correct about the operational cost: a canonicalization disagreement and a forgery both reach us as one Ed25519 verify returning false, and a clock-ahead signer reading our reason name is told the opposite of what is wrong. That is the argument for your set, landing in exactly the layer it is trying to name.

On your un-vectorable tag contradiction, a third datapoint rather than a resolution: we take the RFC 9421 Section 3.2.1 branch. A signature tagged with another protocol is reported invalid, never treated as unsigned. Two honest caveats. The check sits in our step 1, before any directory I/O, so we chose that branch for pipeline reasons, cheap checks first, and did not know we were picking a side. And we report it under the wrong name, since the header is well formed and merely declares a different protocol. There is also a third position the draft does not draw: a gateway that speaks several agent protocols reads the tag to decide which verifier to run, before any of them concludes anything, so for a gateway an unrecognised tag is routing, not an outcome. The contradiction may be sharper for a single-protocol origin.

Correcting something I said on Aug 26. Our verifier does attach a conclusive flag to every result it emits, and the three could-not-check reasons are the only ones that ever carry false. But I said our schema enforces the pairing, and it does not. The field is optional on the type, independent of the reason, and coherence is maintained by hand at seven call sites and by review. Nothing would catch a new could-not-check reason that silently inherited the default. That is a large part of why I want the pairing in the vector schema: yours is enforced by generate.mjs and verify.mjs, and ours is a convention.

On vendoring: the three regressions live in our suite now, and I will pin your JSON the moment a set lands in the draft, the way we did with E.2.3. Until then it is your file, and it has already earned its keep.

issues.title: Relation to OAuth 2
issues.author: thibmeu
issues.body:
There has been a couple of feedback about why not use OAuth 2, DPoP, maybe OIDC in general. We should consider having a section in the appendix to address that.

From the top of my head:
* This is similar indeed: one standard which we scope specifically for bots, with a tag/purpose, key ID definition
* HTTP Message Signatures provides @authority derived component
* The use of JWK Thumbprint as keyid is sufficient. No need for DPoP
* DPoP is specifically addressing replay and access refresh
* The Authorization server is the client, which seems to be closer to HTTP Message Signatures design
* Extensibility to allow request integrity and non-repudiability with HTTP Message Signatures, possibly with mulitple ones

comments.author: thibmeu
comments.body:
From @garyillyes on the [mailing list](https://mailarchive.ietf.org/arch/msg/web-bot-auth/JHZcHwwYlOt_y1T_YcENGP5yAnM/): consideration about [SPIFFE](https://spiffe.io/). Trying to recall the differences from the top of my head before i log out for the day and reply on the mailing:

1. I understand SPIFFE as being based on trust domain. Signature-Agent helps with that discovery to avoid a central registry for a public web.
2. Transitivity is a nice property of HTTP Sigs
3. There is no binding to a specific authority, or headers, like with HTTP Sigs. This is a nice to have
4. There is an ongoing thread on [oauth mailing list](https://mailarchive.ietf.org/arch/msg/oauth/3dpBuZqHRxlx33AyTZNUqofnM_0/) about dynamic registration with OAuth using SPIFFE sharing some of the properties

TLDR is registration is covered with Signature-Agent allowing for multiple trust domains. SPIFFE would be interesting to provide that unique workload URL, and possibly identify a specific workload instead of their principals.

Hello!
I've spoken with @thibmeu around this and he asked me to add our (BBC) current-known use case. I _think_ this is probably the most appropriate existing issue but please let me know if you want me to move it.

We have some folks in BBC Studios who are looking at the potential for licensing our content (or subsets of it) for use in various ways e.g. LLM training, paid-for reformatting/summarisation etc.

Right now, we use robots.txt where we can in the usual/standard way but this is a seriously poor whack-a-mole experience from our PoV because:

* Bot documentation quality is extremely variable so it's not always easy/possible to work out what a specific bot's intent (purpose) is

This'd obviously be a divergence from the current robots.txt system which lists per-bot/UA tokens but it would be so much more manageable.

Hope all that makes sense!

issues.title: Add wording that `Signature` header  MUST be sent over a secure connection
issues.author: jhoyla
issues.body: Because the `Signature` header is effectively a bearer token, and can be proxied, and in some cases replayed, there needs to be a `MUST` requiring that the `Signature` header is always sent (and proxied) over secure (esp. confidential) channels.

comments.author: thibmeu
comments.body:
A possible text from [RFC 6750 Section 5.3](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc6750#section-5.3)

> Always use TLS (https):  Clients MUST always use TLS [[RFC5246](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc5246)]
> (https) or equivalent transport security when making requests with
> bearer tokens.  Failing to do so exposes the token to numerous

comments.body:
We also need text on the use of proxies. Something along the lines of:
> If forwarding a request containing a `Signature` header to a different party, a proxy MUST either use TLS or equivalent protection to talk to both the sender and receiver, or strip the `Signature` header. issues.title: Use signature label to identity signature instead of tab
issues.author: leelynne
issues.body:
I wanted to suggest using the signature label to identity the signature for validation instead of using the tag. This is also feedback I will give to the http signature spec itself.

The main reason is because it is valid to have multiple signatures with the same tag but not with the same label. Multiple tags introduces variance between implementations when doing single signature validation and the latter does not.

The observation is that while there can be multiple signatures present on a request each signature is typically intended for one purpose. In my companies case that purpose is for workload authentication - there should be only one of these for the direct caller.  Similarly Amazon Seller central expects one signature for a request for third-party payment providers [1].

As an implementer of HTTP signatures [2] we have had to create an interface to allow library users to select the one signature they want to validate and ignore the others.  If you allow them to specify a tag as the selector then the HTTP signatures implementation has to make a choice of how to handle requests with multiple signatures with the same tag.  Take the first one as returned by the parser?  Take the first one ordered by key id? Return an error? Validate them all?

In contrast each signature must have a unique label (or else it is not valid structured field dictionary [3] and should fail to parse).

It is still true that signature validators should not assign special meaning to the signature label however as a selector it does exactly what it should do without ambiguity.


[1] - https://developer-docs.amazon.com/sp-api/docs/tpp-registration-signature-guidance
[2] - https://github.com/remitly-oss/httpsig-go
[3] - https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc8941#name-dictionaries

comments.author: thibmeu
comments.body:
Is the idea that labels are simpler to filter on?

I have the impression that we could ask for a label to be put, but I'm not sure the function is the same as a tag. A tag can be used as a filter, even if there are multiple signatures. This is a desirable subset of HTTP Message Signatures.

I agree that it defers the decision to select signatures to implementers. In some cases, being able to select multiple signatures is actually desirable.

Each company can decide to put a unique identifying label. This is what [AWS seems to do](https://developer-docs.amazon.com/sp-api/docs/tpp-registration-signature-guidance) with label `x-amzn-psd2`.

Also, as @jricher mentioned on [web-bot-auth](https://mailarchive.ietf.org/arch/msg/web-bot-auth/lFJ5GKrFAKHL9qF6oAtTPv8TLMQ/) mailinglist, labels are not included in the signing material. This is a property we would like to have proper bindings.

issues.title: Add HTTP Status Code Specifications for Signature Verification Errors
issues.author: gauribaraskar
issues.body:
Since web bot auth architecture is an application of HTTP Message Signatures, as defined in [RFC 9421 section 1.4](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9421#section-1.4), the draft should specify appropriate HTTP status codes for signature verification failures. Currently, section 4.4 references the verification algorithm but doesn't specify what status codes origins should return for different failure scenarios. 

We could add a new section specifying appropriate HTTP status codes for different failure scenarios:
1. 401 Unauthorized: Missing/invalid/expired signatures, unknown keyid
2. 403 Forbidden: Valid signature but access denied by policy
3. 400 Bad Request: Malformed headers, missing required components, invalid tag, reusing nonce

issues.title: Add Key binding consideration in directory draft
issues.author: thibmeu
issues.body:
It could be useful for keys to be binded to a domain. There are multiple approaches that could be used, and I'm not sure which one should be mandated, if any. Possible approaches I see at the moment

1. /.well-known/... to be served with one/more HTTP Message Signature over the digest and `@authority` 
2. have a challenge mechanism for updates/key liveness
3. have an identity string as part of JWK. It could be via x5c if leveraging certificates associated to a signature-agent, or a new field
4. Require bots to register their keys as part of a global root (similar to webpki)

It would be great if these process allow for key mirroring.

comments.author: cjpatton
comments.body: Can you clarify what the goal is in binding a key to a domain? If to associate some well known identity to the bot: is domain always an appropriate form of identity?

comments.author: jhoyla
comments.body: I think 1 could be fine, assuming the domain is also in the signed portion.

comments.author: jhoyla
comments.body: Maybe realm is more flexible than domain?

comments.author: thibmeu
comments.body:
The goal of binding to a domain is to ensure that when consuming a directory, you still preserve the domain it was served from.

If you have two bots a and b with keyA and keyB, bot b may serve keyA in its directory.
And when validating keyA, you may be unable to tell if it's the key of bot a or bot b, even though only bot a is able to produce such signatures.

Therefore you need a binding to ensure keyA is always associated to bot a


This is specific to the directory, therefore using domains. The architecture works with keyid that a client trusts. You can define other retrieval mechanism that would work fine as long as you have confidence that the key uniquely identifies a bot.

issues.author: thibmeu

HTTP Message Signatures relies on strwuctured field to canonicalise an HTTP request.
Structured fields allow for two different inputs to be canonicalised to the same string.

There are considerations around this in HTTP Message Signatures [RFC 9421, Section 7.5.2](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9421#section-7.5.2).

At minimum, the architecture draft has to restate these.

There is an open question if the architecture should place additional rules which are not part of HTTP Message Signatures.

issues.title: Binding a public key to an identity possible with x5c chaining (rogue key attacks)
issues.author: EthanHeilman
issues.body:
This may not be a concern for this use case  but wanted to make a note of it.

Since the JWK isn't covered by the HTTP message signature it is possible to do a rogue key attack where you associate someone else's public key with your own identity. These attacks don't break signature forgability because you aren't able to create new signatures under that key, but there are cases in some protocols where the confusion between public key and identity may result in harm.

1. See JWK and HTTP signature for identity example.com
2. Sign x509 cert for evil.com with public key from JWK and replay HTTP signature.

The replay attack doesn't violate your security model, but someone might be able to bind a public key which they don't know the signing key for to their identity. I don't think the x509 format protects against rogue keys, but I could be wrong

issues.title: Clarify or remove "purpose" in/from section 4.5., Key Distribution and Discovery
issues.author: garyillyes
issues.body:
There's a new "purpose" field in the example key in [section 4.5., Key Distribution and Discovery](https://www.ietf.org/archive/id/draft-meunier-web-bot-auth-architecture-03.html#name-key-distribution-and-discov).

The field should be either: 
1. clarified and properly referenced (e.g., ai-pref drafts), or
2. removed, because considering that once the request is signed the rest of the headers can be de-facto trusted, so perhaps the "purpose" field should be outside the JSON 

Alternatively, the language in the section should be phrased as an example, such as `Implementers MAY add new fields from a IANA registry to the <JSON>; for example, "purpose" in the following example.`

IMO it should be removed. It's unclear that the existence of this field is useful in the key, instead, the purpose of a client should be advertised in other headers (and hopefully WG ai-pref will deal with that)

comments.author: sandormajor
comments.body:
Re option 2: I would not rely on a defacto trust, I think if a new header is added then it will need to be signed by the agent as well. I would maybe even note it somewhere that the verifier should not trust unsigned parts of the message.

Otherwise I agree that the purpose field in the key file is a bit odd and can also be confused with the `use` field that "[identifies the intended use of the public key](https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/rfc7517#section-4.2)". It can be an easy way to share some information about a particular agent, instead of sending it over on every request and signing it, but it might make sense to discuss in a separate document. That doc could go into the details of how it's linked with aipref, what are the available options, provide examples, etc. I saw for instance in some key files very broad purposes like "ai" – if these are not defined somewhere then I think the utility of this field will not be too high.

comments.author: sandormajor
comments.body:
On a related note: [section 5.6. Key Reuse Considered Harmful](https://www.ietf.org/archive/id/draft-meunier-web-bot-auth-architecture-03.html#name-key-reuse-considered-harmfu) also refers to "purposes" but it seems to be different from the one in the `purpose` field. For very large scale systems it might also not be feasible to issue a new identity for every service that might send web requests. If it's a must to issue fine grained identities then I would prefer the SPIFFE-style naming where the workload's identity is in the path and not the domain.

In general, I think the protocol should not prescribe how to shard or group various identities. It's good to highlight the risks of using a mega identity for everything, or to provide guidelines/examples, but requesting it as a must might not work in practice. Or at least it would require a good definition of a "purpose".

issues.title: Clarification on 5.7.  Reverse proxy consideration
issues.author: sandormajor
issues.body:
[5.7. ](https://www.ietf.org/archive/id/draft-meunier-web-bot-auth-architecture-03.html#section-5.7)[Reverse proxy consideration](https://www.ietf.org/archive/id/draft-meunier-web-bot-auth-architecture-03.html#name-reverse-proxy-consideration) says "It implies that the proxy sees the Signature before the origin does, may strip it, or even attempt to replay it against other reverse proxies used by the origin."

1) I think this should have something like "proxies SHOULD NOT (or MUST NOT) strip the `Signature` and `Signature-Agent` headers"
2) Can you please elaborate on "[Origins may require a specific nonce policy](https://www.ietf.org/archive/id/draft-meunier-web-bot-auth-architecture-03.html#name-reverse-proxy-consideration:~:text=Origins%20may%20require%20a%20specific%20nonce%20policy)"? Maybe linking to [5.3. ](https://www.ietf.org/archive/id/draft-meunier-web-bot-auth-architecture-03.html#section-5.3)[Nonce validation](https://www.ietf.org/archive/id/draft-meunier-web-bot-auth-architecture-03.html#name-nonce-validation) is enough but an example could be helpful too.
3) "to prevent such malicious behaviour" implies that the nonce can prevent both replay of the signatures, and the striping of them. They can help with replays but if the proxy strips the signature the best an origin can do is to reject the request with an `accept-signature` response, and maybe provide a nonce itself to challenge the agent. But that would require an extra roundtrip. So I think for striping we should at least have some wording like in point 1

2. even though a client generates a random nonce, an origin may want specific freshness, or for the nonce to be derived from certain parameters (the current date, the previous nonce, others)
3. the sentence indeed implies a second round trip with accept-signature. probably worth adding

issues.title: Consider a mechanism for identifiers (and abuse reporting)
issues.author: chhamilton
issues.body:
Consider the following two examples:

(1) A single customer spins up 1000 instances of an agent to automate actions against ticketseller.com to try to buy tickets to a concert for resale.
(2) 1000 customers each spin up 1 instance of an agent to automate actions against ticketseller.com to try to buy tickets to a concert for personal use.

These both look indentical to ticketseller.com (or its designated security service provider). While there's some amount of responsibility of the agent platform to try restrict abuse of their platform, security platforms also have their role to play. If these standards provide the ability for each signatory (in this case the platform operator) to encode a pseudonymous customer identifier, it makes it easy to distinguish between (1) and (2). It also enables downstream security service providers to build per-customer reputation tracking. For the purposes of anti-abuse it's fine for these to be pseudonymous, and to rotate with some mid-term frequency (O(weeks) is probably fine)?

This also creates the ability for collaborative policing. You could imagine creating an abuse reporting endpoint (can be advertised by the platform operator's metadata in their .wellknown file) where websites and/or security providers can inform the platform operator of abusive actions that were made against a site. Having a well defined identifiers allows them to reference specific actions made by their platform.

If a pseudonymous customer identifier is too much to ask for, at the very least an anonymous session identifier could play the role of grouping together semantically related requests as well as providing an identifier for abuse reporting.

For abuse reporting, I was thinking of something spiritually similar to ARF for spam email.

issues.title: Remove rfc7638 requirement from `keyid` and make it match `kid`
issues.author: sandormajor
issues.body:
Both [HTTP Message Signatures for automated traffic Architecture](https://thibmeu.github.io/http-message-signatures-directory/draft-meunier-web-bot-auth-architecture.html) and [HTTP Message Signatures Directory](https://thibmeu.github.io/http-message-signatures-directory/draft-meunier-http-message-signatures-directory.html) says

> `keyid` MUST be a base64url JWK SHA-256 Thumbprint as defined in [Section 3.2](https://rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc7638#section-3.2) of [[JWK-THUMBPRINT](https://thibmeu.github.io/http-message-signatures-directory/draft-meunier-web-bot-auth-architecture.html#JWK-THUMBPRINT)] for RSA and EC, and in [Appendix A.3](https://rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc8037#appendix-A.3) of [[JWK-OKP](https://thibmeu.github.io/http-message-signatures-directory/draft-meunier-web-bot-auth-architecture.html#JWK-OKP)] for ed25519

I would change "MUST" here to "MAY". Key management systems often have IDs for their keys already so they could just print them here from a DB, instead of constructing and serializing a temporary JWK into a json and hashing that per rfc7638, then adding it back to the structure and serializing again. The Tink library also seems to have a notion of a [Key ID](https://developers.google.com/tink/wire-format#tink_output_prefix), and I also like that it's 4 bytes, instead of 32 like the SHA256. People might also use dates or other examples used in the rfc7638 or rfc9421, I think that's fine as long as it helps finding the key in the dictionary.

The specs could also say that `keyid` and `kid` should match between an entry of the JWKS and the`Signature-Input`, to speed up verification, otherwise verifiers might drop the request.

comments.author: thibmeu
comments.body:
Using JWK Thumbprint as the keyid guarantees global uniqueness. This brings nice properties like not having to think about conflict or ID reuses.

My impression is that's valuable, and thumbprint calculation could be done a-priori and stored in a DB as a field if needed. kid can have different information such as a date, and that's totally acceptable.

Having the kid be the JWK Thumbprint is actually a recommendation from various applications of JWK (openid [for instance](https://openid.net/specs/openid-federation-1_0.html#section-8.7.2-5.6.3.2)). That's what I'd recommend to set as well, rather than staying with arbitrary kid.

Trying to find the reason for that specific ask: does it come down to kid likely being set and stored, vs jwk thumbprint usually being computed rather than stored?

comments.author: sandormajor
comments.body:
> Using JWK Thumbprint as the keyid guarantees global uniqueness. This brings nice properties like not having to think about conflict or ID reuses.

It helps verifiers a little bit because they could use the thumbprint alone to look up keys in their cache, they would need to add at least the domain to the cache otherwise. On the other hand, the current spec forces the signer to adapt a particular type of ID + send 32 bytes over the wire on every request.

To use a concrete example: at Google thousands of engineers are using a keystore implementation that has its own notion of a key id. I can get a key, sign the request with it and send it out in about 3 lines of code. The key id is unique within a keyset which is enough for the verifiers to avoid trying out all the keys in the directory (if `keyId = kid`), but the key size is 1/8 of the SHA256.
If I need to use the JWK Thumbprint I'm not going to add it to that keystore system, so now instead of 3 lines of code I need to bring up a database to cache the thumbprints with their actual key IDs, manage this cache, have extra roundtrips to look it up, and then send an 8x larger ID on every request. We're talking about potentially millions of requests per second, so the id length alone could add terabytes of data transferred per day.

> My impression is that's valuable, and thumbprint calculation could be done a-priori and stored in a DB as a field if needed. kid can have different information such as a date, and that's totally acceptable.

The rfc9421 says the `keyid` is "The identifier for the key material as a String value", and the rfc7517 says `kid` is "used to match a specific key [...] for instance, to choose among a set of keys within a JWK Set" – I think it would be really bad if the `kid` in the JWKS could be different from the `keyid` of the `Signature-Input`. And if something, I'm more worried about the `keyid` of the header because that needs to be set for every request (see the previous point re unnecessary caching complexity and payload size)

> Having the kid be the JWK Thumbprint is actually a recommendation from various applications of JWK (openid [for instance](https://openid.net/specs/openid-federation-1_0.html#section-8.7.2-5.6.3.2)). That's what I'd recommend to set as well, rather than staying with arbitrary kid.

I'm fine with a recommendation ("SHOULD") but a "MAY" is more appropriate in my opinion. I'm not convinced that adding 32 bytes on every signed request on the web is justified.

> Trying to find the reason for that specific ask: does it come down to kid likely being set and stored, vs jwk thumbprint usually being computed rather than stored?

It comes down to accepting the key ID provided by signers. The goal of the `keyid` of the `Signature-Input` is to help identify a `kid` within the `Signature-Agent`'s current keyset, I would leave it up to the signer to decide how they generate that id. There will be numerous participants of the ecosystem who are already dealing with keys but were not concerned about JWK Thumbprints so far. Forcing all of them to adapt it, and forcing everyone to use unreasonably long IDs has a lot more downsides, in my opinion, than there are benefits of globally unique IDs

comments.author: thibmeu
comments.body:
Signature-Agent is optional (despite RECOMMENDED). You are right that, as defined by [RFC 9421 Section 2.3](https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/rfc9421#signature-params), keyid is `The identifier for the key material as a String value`. It does not say it should be kid. In fact, kid is optional per [RFC 7515](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc7517.html#section-4.5).
An identifier may even just be the order of the key: key 0, key 1, etc.

Setting it to the thumbprint guarantees global uniqueness, and discovery in the presence or absence of a Signature-Agent.

On your mention of
> I'm not going to add it to that keystore system
is the blocker internal process?

Would a wording you'd be after be

comments.body:
> Signature-Agent is optional (despite RECOMMENDED). It does not say it should be kid. In fact, kid is optional per [RFC 7515](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc7517.html#section-4.5). Yes, `kid` is optional per the rfc but I think this spec could introduce new constraints. E.g. if it specifies how the keys are distributed, it could ask for the `keyid` to match the `kid`.

> Setting it to the thumbprint guarantees global uniqueness, and discovery in the presence or absence of a Signature-Agent.

That's a good point, I haven't really thought of out-of-band key sharing. I think in that case enforcing a certain ID type is even worse. In that case it's up to the parties involved to agree on the key format, key type, and how to share the keys – why would we enforce a certain key ID type? They might not even use a JWK format.

> On your mention of
> 
> > I'm not going to add it to that keystore system
> > is the blocker internal process?

No, processes could add probably months of lead time, that would be unfortunate of course, but the more problematic part is that this system is not concerned about JWKs or various serializations of the keys, it doesn't really belong there. If I would own the service (and I wouldn't have concerns about the ID length) I would add it, but since this is a gigantic horizontal people will have strong opinions about it. This is not unique to Google btw, this is a problem people using common keystores will have. E.g. if you're using GCP's Cloud KMS you won't be able to store the thumbprint in KMS either (maybe as labels but that would be odd). You also can't subscribe to key rotation events so you'd need to parse audit logs with Eventarc or something, or just keep fetching the keys to detect changes. I think AWS KMS might have events for key rotation but it also can't store the thumbprint so teams would need to store them somewhere else.

> Would a wording you'd be after be
> 
> > When a Signature-Agent is provided, `kid` MUST be set for every key and `keyid` SHOULD equal to a kid in the directory

I'd change the SHOULD to a MUST, maybe with the caveat "if there are multiple keys in the directory". I think the `keyid` must tell which key to use from the keyset, but if there's a single key then there's no point in sending the `keyid`.

issues.title: Interesting (mis)use of Web Bot Auth
issues.author: sandormajor
issues.body:
I ran across [this article](https://chrisleverseo.com/blog/how-to-fix-shopify-crawl-issues-in-screaming-frog-and-sitebulb-using-web-bot-auth/). This might be the first attempt of someone implementing delegation.

Shopify [uses](https://help.shopify.com/en/manual/promoting-marketing/seo/crawling-your-store) WBA to allow crawlers back to stores hosted by Shopify itself. This doesn't seem to be better than using oldschool API keys, but introduces a lot of unnecessary payload and extra hops to fetch Shopify's own public key (that will not change ever anyway because everyone will hardcode the signatures in the requests of their 3P tools).

I think WBA's goal in a scenario like this should be to identify the crawler (e.g. "screamingfrog.co.uk", or "sitebulb.com") and not Shopify itself. The user could then select on the Shopify UI which bots to allow, without all the manual copy-pasting and hardcoding signatures. The signatures meant to be short lived and ideally used once. The signatures issued by Shopify have no expiry and no nonce, a leaked signature can be used forever to crawl a store. Even if the user manually rotates the signatures, thinking it's kind of a token, the verification will succeed until the public key is rotated. And the signing key can leak too, so rotating it is required. WBA provides a nice key-publishing mechanism through the .well-known file, but updating that now would mean that Shopify will need to break all the integrations of all their customers. All users would need to go back and manually generate a new signature using the new key and update them at all their 3Ps. The `exp` of [their key](https://www.shopify.com/.well-known/http-message-signatures-directory) is July next year so they might have a breakage around that time.

I think to avoid such misuse the spec should say that the signing agent MUST rotate the keys at least daily, and signatures MUST have an expiry shorter than X – e.g. 5 minutes.

If the goal of Shopify here was to kind of "approve" a request sent by someone else, then issuing a certificate for the crawler and then letting the crawler sign the request with their own signing key would be a better approach, but I'm not sure if that's even necessary here.

Edit: There might be some expiry on the signature, I realized it's masked out on the screenshot, and the [docs](https://help.shopify.com/en/manual/promoting-marketing/seo/crawling-your-store#:~:text=Set%20signatures%20to%20expire%20after%20a%20specific%20period.%20The%20maximum%20period%20is%203%20months) say "Set signatures to expire after a specific period. The maximum period is 3 months". Which is a bit odd because the users will need to manually rotate these signatures. And I think 3 months is too long.

comments.author: thibmeu
comments.body:
The initial intent of WBA is indeed to have crawler self-identifying themselves.

Using Signature-Agent as a convenient way to distribute signatures and an allowed registration mechanism is quite interesting indeed. In a way, it works similar to webhook authentication. There is an authentication you'll need to handle in the future, and instead of an arbitrary bearer you use HTTP Sigs to carry this.

Two actions that could help down the line:
* [Key rotation is a recommendation](https://thibmeu.github.io/http-message-signatures-directory/draft-meunier-http-message-signatures-directory.html#name-key-rotation). I don't think we can actually make it mandatory with a MUST, but it'd be worth highlighting in a best practice document
* Have a clear [delegation story](https://thibmeu.github.io/http-message-signatures-directory/draft-meunier-http-message-signatures-directory.html#name-delegation-and-chaining). The directory draft provides a couple of examples, but does not have a preferred mechanism. I think it would help here. Again, part of a best practice document.

Side: Both do seem relevant for wimse working group as well.

comments.author: sandormajor
comments.body:
I agree, this seems similar to a webhook auth, but I'd argue it is worse because of the above mentioned reasons. I think it would be great – both for this specific case and for the delegation story – to understand what their intent was.

Regarding the actions:

1. Since this is a new protocol I think this is the best time to make it mandatory. Why do you think it might not work? Once people start aligning with a lax requirement it will be impossible to make it more strict. Going the other way is easier. Frequent key rotation can avoid lots of issues, just think of a key you might deploy to your domain today to play with the protocol, then 10 years later with all the other protocols built around web-bot-auth you somehow become liable for something someone did with your key you long forgot about. I would maybe even go so far as to say that verifiers MUST NOT accept keys older than a certain time frame. Obviously a text will not prevent people from misimplementing it but I think the spec should be clear that key rotation is a must.
2. I'm not sure delegation is really needed here. It would be great to ask Shopify if you talk to them. But otherwise I agree that it would be great to have some guidelines for delegation. I will think more about it.

comments.author: madmath
comments.body:
Hi, I'm from Shopify and worked on the implementation. Our non-technical end users are using various tools (e.g. automated crawlers, accessibility audit tools) to access their sites hosted on Shopify, and it seemed unreasonable to ask these tools to implement web-bot-auth signing logic (some are native applications with unclear release cycles) and even then, it would have implied that the users possibly input a private key into the software (as we wouldn't want all users of a piece of software to identify as the same party, e.g. `crawling-software.com`). Adding custom headers on the other hand is fairly well supported in this particular software ecosystem (and even down to `curl`). 

We are intending to re-use web-bot-auth verification infrastructure to detect other parties that are hitting Shopify infra (similar to how Cloudflare are verifying requests from AI crawlers). And we may expand this program to identify software partners in the future.

I understand that we are using message signatures / the web-bot-auth extension in a slightly bifurcated way (for users hitting their own sites), but I'm unclear why that is an issue or whether that is less secure than an equivalent solution of expiring API keys. 

As far as our public key expiring eventually, before the deadline we will introduce an additional public key and stop generating signatures with the old one. 

Thanks

comments.author: sandormajor
comments.body:
Thanks @madmath for chiming in! See my replies below.

> Hi, I'm from Shopify and worked on the implementation. Our non-technical end users are using various tools (e.g. automated crawlers, accessibility audit tools) to access their sites hosted on Shopify, and it seemed unreasonable to ask these tools to implement web-bot-auth signing logic (some are native applications with unclear release cycles) and even then, it would have implied that the users possibly input a private key into the software (as we wouldn't want all users of a piece of software to identify as the same party, e.g. `crawling-software.com`). Adding custom headers on the other hand is fairly well supported in this particular software ecosystem (and even down to `curl`).

If crawlers want to support multiple tenants, they can issue identities like `[customer].crawling-software.com`, or you could simply mint "tokens" or API keys for your users that they would add as a custom header (e.g. `X-Shopify-Crawler-Key`). I see that adding custom headers is simple but you're asking your users to add a header that is used for something different. It's a bit like asking your users to replace the `User-Agent` header with something custom, you can certainly do that but I would advise against it.

> We are intending to re-use web-bot-auth verification infrastructure to detect other parties that are hitting Shopify infra (similar to how Cloudflare are verifying requests from AI crawlers). And we may expand this program to identify software partners in the future.

The problem is that you might have thousands of users who will manually add `Signature-Agent` (SA) headers with a `Signature` signing over the SA string. That means in the future if `crawling-software.com` would want to integrate with web-bot-auth (the standard way) they will not be able to; your headers will invalidate each other's signatures; or one of you will need to override the other's headers.
Issue https://github.com/thibmeu/http-message-signatures-directory/issues/70 should address the problem of having multiple SA headers but you will still need to ask _all_ your users to update _all_ their integrations to only sign over a particular value within the SA dictionary. I think this also demonstrates why relying on such a manual rollout is problematic. Also note that the spec is in a draft state so there might be more breaking changes coming in the future.

I would still advise agains using WBA this way but this would address most of my compatibility concerns. The other thing you might want to do is changing the `sig1` key in the `Signature`/`Signature-Input` headers. That key is used by all the examples so there will be a high chance of collision.

> I understand that we are using message signatures / the web-bot-auth extension in a slightly bifurcated way (for users hitting their own sites), but I'm unclear why that is an issue or whether that is less secure than an equivalent solution of expiring API keys.

Right, "users hitting their own sites" is why I'm not sure you actually need WBA here. Why does this work better for you than a traditional API key? Now your users need to add 3 weird headers (`Signature`, `Signature-Input`, and `Signature-Agent`), instead of adding a single `X-Shopify-Crawler-Key` header that you do whatever with. Then later if the third-parties (3P) like `crawling-software.com` wants to integrate with WBA then they can just sign requests as the 3P and you'll have a single-click configuration on the merchant's admin UI to grant them access – without all the header voodoo and manual key rotations.

Security I guess depends on your definition of it. People will not want to rotate signatures every day manually so they will likely use the max 3 month TTL. If a signature like that leaks (e.g. by the aforementioned non-technical end users) then whoever has the signature can impersonate Shopify when calling a particular store. I don't know how bad that would be.

Then what if the user actually realizes that their signature leaked? E.g. they see a lot of weird requests scraping their site with the signature, what can they do? They can naively go to the admin UI and generate a new signature and update it at their 3Ps, but that would not invalidate the old signatures. The verifier will check the expiry (which is potentially 3 months), and it will verify the signature using the single, centrally-hosted Shopify key. So if the user is a bit more tech-savvy they will call you to rotate the key but that means you'll need to ask _all_ your customers to update _all_ their integrations because you updated the single key everyone is using. I would not want to bother my customers with this.

> As far as our public key expiring eventually, before the deadline we will introduce an additional public key and stop generating signatures with the old one.

How would you introduce the additional public key? If I got this right then – if I would be your non-techy user – I would generate a signature once, set the expiry to 3 months, then some time before the expiry (if I don't forget it) go back, generate a new signature, and update 2 of the 3 headers at all my 3Ps. Is that correct? If that's right, then key expiry would mean that there's another N month cycle (that's likely out of sync with my 3-month signature rotation cycle) that I need to be aware of, plus there might be unscheduled rotations (see above). I'm not sure I would like that as a user.

One way you could mitigate this _somewhat_ is to "shard" your identity per store, similarly to the 3P example above, e.g. `[store].shopify.com` instead of the global `shopify.com` identity. Then you might be able to remove signature expiry and only deal with key expiry. But that would still mean "Store XYZ calling Store XYZ", instead of "Shopify calling Store XYZ" – None of them is correct because in reality it should be "Crawling-Software calling Store XYZ". Maybe `[3p].[store].shopify.com` would be better but I don't think there's a good reason going down that rabbit hole.

> Thanks

Thanks to you again! It is very important in this early stage of the protocol to gather feedback from people trying solve their problems with it, so I appreciate your response. Let me know if I'm missing something, to me it seems that you don't really need WBA for this and it just introduces more problems than it solves. If you want something that scales better and solves the key rotation problems then WBA can be a good option, but then I think the 3Ps need to authenticate with WBA, not Shopify.

issues.title: Change `Signature-Agent` to a sf-dictionary
issues.author: sandormajor
issues.body:
Currently `Signature-Agent` is a string so there's no relation of it to the signatures, and you also can't sign `Signature-Agent` if different parties add headers with this name. I propose converting the SA header to a dictionary and linking a particular signature to a specific agent, e.g. like this:
```
Signature-Input: sig1=(... "signature-agent";key="sig1");...
Signature: sig1=:3ase6A==:

Signature-Input: sig2=(... "signature-agent";key="sig2");...
Signature: sig2=:3ase6A==:

Signature-Agent: sig1="https://example.com"
Signature-Agent: sig2="https://agent.example"
```

Or maybe something like
```
Signature-Input: sig1=(... "signature-agent";key="agent1");signature-agent=agent1;...
Signature-Agent: agent1="https://example.com"
```

comments.author: thibmeu
comments.body:
I like the idea and there seems to be a clear need for it.

If we believe the set of keys is going to be small, we could also mandate that `signature-agent` is keyed with the same label as the `signature` and `signature-input`. Example looks similar to your first proposal, as follow

```
Signature-Input: sig1=(... "signature-agent");...
Signature: sig1=:3ase6A==:

Signature-Input: sig2=(... "signature-agent");...
Signature: sig2=:3ase6A==:

Signature-Agent: sig1="https://example.com"
Signature-Agent: sig2="https://agent.example"
```


cf #32

comments.body: I like both of these approaches. The key/alias idea is flexible and could support multiple mappings per signature, while the label-keyed dictionary is simpler, fully RFC 9421-compliant, and easier to parse and maintain.

The proposal I made does not seem to satisfy them both.

I opened a PR with @sandormajor 's proposal, both for the directory and the architecture. It's in #71

One thing I'm not sure about is whether we need the `sf` flag, e.g.

The spec currently says that `@authority` [MUST](https://thibmeu.github.io/http-message-signatures-directory/draft-meunier-web-bot-auth-architecture.html#section-4.2-3.2.1) be signed. Technically one could reuse a nonce but they probably shouldn't

comments.author: thibmeu
comments.body:
I think the two are different, but the two recommendations may create a conflict indeed. Would your recommendation be to not use a nonce if you replay your signatures?

The nonce is a discussion we could have with the group. The proposal [draft-hoypat-httpbis-message-signatures-ekm](https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/draft-hoypat-httpbis-message-signatures-ekm/) from @cjpatton and @jhoyla improves the security model for deployment that don't want replayability for instance.

comments.author: sandormajor
comments.body:
Yes I think reusing the nonce is not correct and it might break some implementations that expect a nonce to be seen only once, even if they would otherwise allow replays in the absence of a nonce.

The TLS binding sounds interesting but that would introduce some of the same problems as a purely TLS-based authentication would have. E.g. proxies terminating TLS would prevent the origin to validate the signature. The proposal mentions
>    If they do not share a direct TLS connection, it is possible to
   architect a system such that the verifier does not directly call the
   exporter interface, but is simply provided its output on a trusted

If the verifier and caller trust each other then the same system could be used with mTLS  without HTTP signatures

issues.title: Relabelling proxy MAY break signature-agent signatures
issues.author: thibmeu
issues.body:
[Section 5.7.1 or -architecture-04](https://www.ietf.org/archive/id/draft-meunier-web-bot-auth-architecture-04.html#section-5.7.1) mentions that relabelling can be done by intermediating proxy. This would, however, break the signature-base as the `key` parameter is part of the base.

There has been some discussion on https://github.com/thibmeu/http-message-signatures-directory/pull/71#discussion_r2456224438 and https://github.com/thibmeu/http-message-signatures-directory/pull/71#discussion_r2449178915

Reusing the example,

going from

```
Signature-Agent: agent1="https://signature-agent.test"
Signature-Input: sig1=("signature-agent";key="agent1")
Signature: sig1=:base64==:
```

to 

```
Signature-Agent: SHOULD_MATCH_SIGNATURE_AGENT_KEY="https://signature-agent.test"
Signature-Input: sig1=("signature-agent";key="SHOULD_MATCH_SIGNATURE_AGENT_KEY")
Signature: sig1=:base64==:
```

issues.title: Signature base errors in test vectors
issues.author: jricher
issues.body:
Per Section [2.1.2 of RFC9421](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9421.html#name-dictionary-structured-field), when indicating a single key of a dictionary type field, the component identifier includes the key as a parameter to the string, and the value of the component is the key value alone. 

Currently the example signature bases in A and B are of the form:

```
...
"signature-agent": sig2="https://signature-agent.test"
"@signature-params": ("@authority" "signature-agent";key="sig2")\
...
```

However, to sign the `sig2` key of the `signature-agent` field, it should instead be:

```
...
"signature-agent";key="sig2": "https://signature-agent.test"
"@signature-params": ("@authority" "signature-agent";key="sig2")\
...
```

This same error is repeated in every test vector that uses the `key` modifier for the signed dictionary.

issues.title: [architecture] Verifier must bound resource consumption when fetching key directories
issues.author: thibmeu
issues.body:
Verifiers that fetch key directories from untrusted origins (via Signature-Agent) are exposed to several denial-of-service vectors:

1. **Response size**: a directory can be arbitrarily large. Verifiers should reject responses exceeding a defined byte limit.
2. **Key count**: a JWKS with many keys forces O(n) key search. Verifiers should enforce a maximum key count.
3. **Fetch latency**: no timeout allows slow-loris-style exhaustion. Verifiers should apply a wall-clock timeout to directory fetches.
4. **Redirect chains**: unbounded HTTP redirects can be used to amplify requests. Verifiers should limit redirect depth.

The draft should add normative language (SHOULD/MUST) in the Security Considerations section covering these cases.

Suggested by @motdotla
fyi @sandormajor

issues.title: Implementers to fall back on existing verification methods
issues.author: sandormajor
issues.body:
I ran into issues with multiple verifiers where they treated IP- and WBA-based verification as mutually exclusive. This means that the de facto standards that worked for decades (e.g. [JAFAR](https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/draft-illyes-aipref-jafar/) or FCrDNS) are now expected to be replaced with a new, experimental draft overnight.
I propose amending the spec with something along the lines of "Verifiers MUST fall back to existing verification techniques, such as [JAFAR](https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/draft-illyes-aipref-jafar/) or forward-confirmed reverse DNS (FCrDNS) lookups" – maybe with a todo to revisit this once the spec is standardized.

My tests also ran into multiple verifiers that are out of spec. E.g. they did not implement the breaking change https://github.com/thibmeu/http-message-signatures-directory/pull/71. This combined with the lack of fallbacks means that the old way of verification is effectively deprecated, while the new method is not working yet. Issues like this in my opinion justify the use of MUST instead of a SHOULD.

I also propose adding a big red note on the top of the document asking implementers to subscribe to pull requests on the repo and implement the latest changes in a timely manner.

comments.author: thibmeu
comments.body:
I agree having a proposed fallback would be good.

As for specific method, I think the spec should only point to some, but not be prescriptive. For instance, having run some numbers with JAFAR (and following the spec closely in https://github.com/thibmeu/jafar), it's adopted but not consistent accross providers yet.

For the recommendation to implementers to subscribe to a communication channel, we could have a clear mention at the top

comments.author: bobbiec
comments.body:
As one of those verifiers that does not yet accept the latest WBA version (competing priorities on my team), I also see that many signers have *not updated their signing* to implement the breaking change https://github.com/thibmeu/http-message-signatures-directory/pull/71 . So I expect that verifiers will need to continue to accept multiple versions going forward, at least until the working group aligns to mint an stable "v1". 

Two thoughts here:
* For WBA, the protocol could explicitly include a version number as part of the signed content. Verifiers should accept the latest version and may choose to accept older versions. 
* I think that it would be a little odd to tie WBA to fall back to other verification methods through a MUST - this would mean that for a new verifier, it would be impossible to compliantly implement WBA without implementing JAFAR/FCrDNS even though the technologies are totally unrelated (even though the use cases are similar).

Technically the protocol is versioned by draft (-01, -04), but each draft is independant. That's something we should discuss as implementers. Can be here.

Agree we should not have a MUST on other standards. A recommendation to fallback to existing method if any could still be useful though.

issues.title: Guidance on "http-message-signatures-directory" file & bot-blocking
issues.author: softplus
issues.body:
While implementing web-bot-auth in a personal toy/tool project, I noticed I couldn't verify signatures from chatgpt. It turns out, they are (were at the time of writing) blocking Cloudflare workers from accessing the `http-message-signatures-directory` file. 

The protocol is (afaik) unclear about what to do in such a situation. 

For systems verifying the signature (given a lot of websites that might want to verify the signature are on hosting providers with tainted IP address ranges, I imagine this will happen from time to time):

* Should there be re-tries? At which frequency & for how long?
* Should requests for `http-message-signatures-directory` themselves use web-bot-auth?
* Should these signatures be considered invalid?

For operators providing web-bot-auth headers:

* Is there guidance about how to deal with "bot" requests? Must all requests be serviced?
* Should operators put the file on a host that doesn't use bot-protection?

Should some of this be documented in the protocol? Or is ... dealing with bot blocking considered out of scope for this?

comments.author: thibmeu
comments.body:
Having deployment considerations would be a good additions.

I checked with [RFC9309](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9309.html) if there were any particular guidance. The only line is

```
The rules MUST be accessible in a file named "/robots.txt" (all lowercase) in the top-level path of the service
```

As for the specific points, I would say
1. retries would be god and we could include guidance from [RFC9205](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9205), including `retry-after` conformance for instance
2. requests to the well-known should not have to use web-bot-auth. there is the bootstrap question, and more generally these files should be ok to be exposed as is
3. are you saying that the signatures for which you don't have a public key? if so, they would be non verifiable, and become invalid past the directory expiry.

The idea of a mirror could also be good. It is recommended that the directory is signed with HTTP Message Signatures in the response, which should ease mirror integrations. I'm thinking of [privacy pass mirror](https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/draft-ietf-privacypass-consistency-mirror/) or even integration with [keytrans](https://datatracker.ietf.org/wg/keytrans/about/) down the line

For operators
1. No guidance yet.
2. Ideally these files are as accessible as possible. There are obvious limits for DoS, but bot should be able to access those (i doubt people will manually copy paste these files which we want to update at a regular cadence)

issues.title: proposal: distinguish same-origin TLS binding from delegated signing
issues.author: igrigorik
issues.body:
§5.2 ("Binding keys to the directory authority") RECOMMENDS that a directory server include one per-key HTTP Message Signature over `@authority;req` + `content-digest`, and says *"clients SHOULD ignore keys from a directory response that do not have a corresponding valid signature."* PR #98's intent extends this to `jwks_uri` responses ("we still strongly suggest that jwks_uri response is signed to bind keys to a domain").

This is applied **uniformly**, but the binding goal is already met by the transport in one common case:

- **Same-origin serving.** When the directory / `jwks_uri` is served from the **same origin** as the `@authority` the keys speak for, TLS to that origin already binds the keys to that authority. A verifier that fetched `https://signer.example/...` over TLS and got these keys has the same authority binding the per-key `@authority;req` signature would provide. The signature is redundant with TLS here.

- **Delegated / cross-origin serving.** When keys are served from a **different** origin than the authority (delegation, third-party key hosting, a shared key service), TLS to the key host does **not** bind the keys to the authority. The per-key `@authority;req` signature is then the essential — and only — binding. This is exactly where §5.2 earns its keep.

## Proposal

Scope §5.2's signing recommendation (and the "ignore unsigned keys" guidance) to the **delegated / cross-origin** case, or at minimum add a note that **a directory/`jwks_uri` served same-origin with the authority over TLS satisfies the authority-binding goal without per-key signatures.** Otherwise a conformant verifier following the blanket SHOULD would ignore unsigned keys that are in fact securely bound to the authority by TLS.

## Why it matters

Deployments that reuse a **same-origin identity document as the JWKS** — e.g., an agent/commerce profile served at the operator's own well-known URL, pointed to by `Signature-Agent; type=jwks_uri` — would otherwise be forced into dynamic per-key response signing: private keys at the serving layer (or a precompute pipeline), caches keyed on `@authority`, and re-signing on `expires`. That is real operational burden with **no security gain over TLS** in the same-origin case. Distinguishing the two cases keeps the simple same-origin path viable while preserving the signature requirement where it is actually load-bearing (delegation/cross-origin).

comments.author: thibmeu
comments.body:
> When the directory / jwks_uri is served from the same origin as the @authority the keys speak for, TLS proves the authority served this public key set.

I don't think that's true. Serving key_example on example.com does not prove that example.com has ownership of the key. Because the keys are public, we could imagine evil.example.com serving the same keys.

Serving a signature over the requested authority helps to bind it. That applies both to the delegated and same-origin.


We can clarify section 5.2 to distinguish transport integrity from key-authority binding, but I would not scope the signing recommendation only to cross-origin/delegated discovery. Would that fit better?

comments.author: shivdeep1
comments.body:
> We can clarify section 5.2 to distinguish transport integrity from key-authority binding, but I would not scope the signing recommendation only to cross-origin/delegated discovery. Would that fit better?

Picking this up late because the same scoping question came back on the list this week, and I think the distinction you proposed is the answer to it.

In -02 this text is Appendix B, "Validating the domain binding", and it opens with "It applies to the directory type in Section 5.5."

That's right for the binding. 4.5 rests on the well-known path being reserved, so an arbitrary jwks_uri path can't carry it. But B.1 is a possession proof over @authority and content-digest, and possession isn't type-specific. Two properties sharing one appendix, and the scope sentence reads as covering both.

Practical effect: a jwks_uri or cimd operator can't produce a conformant proof, since 5.5.3 wants "a valid directory response signature as described in Appendix B" and the tag is pinned to `http-message-signatures-directory`. Which cuts against #98, "We still strongly suggest that jwks_uri response is signed to bound keys to a domain."

Two implementers said on the list this week they only do B.1 on directory responses, because that's what the text licenses.

Suggested edit to the scope paragraph:

```
The domain binding described in Section 4.5 applies to the directory type
in Section 5.5. The possession proof in Appendix B.1 is not specific to
that type: it covers @authority and content-digest, and applies to any
response serving key material. A server publishing under jwks_uri or cimd
MAY include it, and a verifier MAY consume it under Section 5.5.3.
```

The tag is the loose end. Simplest is a sentence saying the value names the mechanism rather than the resource, so it's unchanged across types. A second value would be cleaner and more churn. Happy to write either as a PR.

issues.title: [directory] DNS-rooted key discovery: bind the Signature-Agent key with a DANE-EE TLSA record under a DNSSEC-signed name
issues.author: kakooch
issues.body:
## Summary

`draft-meunier-webbotauth-httpsig-directory-00` discovers a bot's signing keys over HTTPS: the `Signature-Agent` value points at an authority, and the verifier fetches `/.well-known/http-message-signatures-directory` (or a `data:` URI) to get the JWKS. Section 4.1 restricts the `Signature-Agent` URI scheme to `https` (RECOMMENDED), `http`, and `data`. Discovery and the key-to-authority binding therefore live entirely in the web PKI and on the web endpoint.

This issue proposes a DNS-rooted option that sits alongside the `.well-known` directory: an authority publishes the SHA-256 of its signing key's SubjectPublicKeyInfo as a DANE-EE (`3 1 1`) TLSA record under a DNSSEC-signed anchoring name (DANE-EE mnemonic RFC 7218; base DANE RFC 6698, updated by RFC 7671). A verifier then confirms the key-to-domain binding from the DNS root, with no `.well-known` fetch and no dependence on whoever currently controls the authority's web endpoint.

## Why an option, not just the HTTPS path

The binding question is already live in this repo:

- **#100** draws the line between same-origin TLS binding and delegated cross-origin signing. In the delegated case, §5.2 leans on a per-key HTTP Message Signature over `@authority;req` to bind keys to the authority. A DNSSEC-rooted TLSA record binds the key to the domain directly, so the delegated case gets a binding root that does not require per-key response signing at the serving layer.
- **#83** wants to drop `http` and keep only `https` and `data`, i.e. the group already recognises that the discovery channel's trust is transport-dependent. DANE moves the binding root off the web endpoint and onto the DNSSEC chain.
- **#93** asks verifiers to fall back to existing DNS methods (FCrDNS, JAFAR). A verifier that already does a reverse or forward DNS check is one lookup away from also reading a TLSA record.
- **#44** notes rogue-key and key-to-identity confusion when the JWK is not itself authenticated. A TLSA record under a DNSSEC-signed name authenticates the key-to-name binding in the DNS answer, not merely next to the key material.
- **#89** (CIMD, closed) shows the directory is open to more than one discovery mechanism. This is one more, rooted in DNS rather than HTTPS.

## Threat-model delta (stated honestly)

An attacker who takes over the authority's web server, or obtains a mis-issued TLS certificate for it, can serve a rogue `.well-known` directory that a verifier will accept. A DNSSEC-signed TLSA binding is not forgeable without breaking the DNS chain of trust for that name. That is a different, and for many operators a higher, bar.

I want to be precise that it is different, not strictly stronger: it moves part of the trust to the DNS operator, the parent zone, and the registrar, and registrar or zone compromise is the corresponding failure mode. The honest framing is "another independent root a verifier MAY require," not "a replacement that removes web-PKI trust."

Two more concessions up front:

- This only helps verifiers that validate DNSSEC and read DNS live. A verifier without a validating resolver gains nothing, so this is a complement keyed off verifier capability, never a mandate.
- TLSA was defined for TLS endpoints. Using it to anchor a `Signature-Agent` signing key is a deliberate reuse of the RRtype as a key-publication record under an anchoring-name convention. A verifier needs the key in SubjectPublicKeyInfo form to compare the `3 1 1` hash; reconstructing SPKI from the directory's JWK is a small, specifiable step.

## Revocation

Revocation is "remove or replace the TLSA record." It propagates within the DNS TTL for validators that query live. It is not an offline or stapled revocation signal, and I am not claiming it is: a verifier that cached or stapled a prior answer will not see the change until the TTL expires.

## We run this in production, and you can dig it right now

[Whisper Security](https://whisper.online) operates [AS219419](https://as219419.net), announcing IPv6 space under a public ASN. We serve DNSSEC-signed forward and reverse zones for per-endpoint IPv6 addresses at /128 granularity, and we publish each endpoint's public key as a DANE-EE (`3 1 1`) TLSA record under a DNSSEC-signed anchoring name bound to a routable address, with reverse (ip6.arpa) and forward names kept consistent, plus RDAP per address (RFC 7480, 9082, 9083).

A live example you can verify with stock tooling, no account and no private CA:

    dig +dnssec TLSA _443._tcp.ae3b051ff3bf7f478.tdc38e7c55bad3306a92b830f9bb1e4f9.agents.whisper.online
    dig +dnssec AAAA ae3b051ff3bf7f478.tdc38e7c55bad3306a92b830f9bb1e4f9.agents.whisper.online
    curl https://rdap.whisper.online/domain/ae3b051ff3bf7f478.tdc38e7c55bad3306a92b830f9bb1e4f9.agents.whisper.online

The TLSA answer comes back DNSSEC-authenticated (AD flag). Nothing here needs Whisper: any operator with a DNSSEC-signed zone can publish the same record.

## The ask

Is the group open to a DNS-rooted binding option for `Signature-Agent`, either as an additional discovery entry in Section 4.5 (Key Distribution and Discovery) or as a referenced companion mechanism? If there is appetite, I will write it up as a short PR against the directory draft rather than prose in a comment.

For the underlying binding convention (anchoring name, SPKI from JWK, ip6.arpa consistency) we have an Internet-Draft we are bringing to the IETF DANCE WG. Its Applicability section frames exactly this case: HTTP Message Signature key directories are fetched over HTTPS only, and a DANE anchor provides a DNS-rooted alternative to the `.well-known` directory. I will link it here once it is on the datatracker.

Kaveh
[Whisper Security](https://whisper.security)

issues.title: Signature Misbinding in httpsig-protocol-00
issues.author: thibmeu
issues.body:
based on https://mailarchive.ietf.org/arch/msg/web-bot-auth/U2q3ey8YuHbi0agZikqJ_7_y9-o/ from @dennisjackson



In 4.2.2 of draft-meunier-webbotauth-httpsig-protocol-00 [1], the draft 
proposes signing signatures:

 > A signer MAY cover selected members from another signature label,
 > including "signature";key=..., "signature-input";key=..., and
 > "signature-agent";key=.... This lets a signer preserve evidence that
 > another signer contributed to the request.

I don't think this is correct.

RFC 9421 7.3.7 'Signing Signature Values' [2] recommends against what's 
described in the draft, because it doesn't bind the message that 
corresponds to the inner signature:

 > While it would seem that this practice would transitively cover the
 > components under the original signature in a verifiable fashion, the 
attacks
 > described in [JACKSON2019] can be used to impersonate a signature output
 > value on an unrelated message.

If you only want to preserve evidence that a message was signed by 
another, you don't need to sign their signature, you just need to 
preserve their signature, message and public key, so removing this text 
and stating that verifiers should check each signature independently 
would work and avoid these footguns.

If you want a stronger property, like 'Party A only signed this message 
because Party B signed it first', that requires some more careful handling.
