issues.title: Anti-replay requirement is backwards (and likely infeasible)
issues.author: martinthomson
issues.body:
> Client[sic] MUST ensure that this nonce is unique for the validity window of the signature, as defined by created and expires attributes.

-- https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/draft-meunier-webbotauth-httpsig-protocol-01#section-5.2.3-4

This is a fine requirement, but the real requirement is that the server maintain a strike register and reject requests with duplicate nonces.  That's a pretty tall ask, for something that is there primarily to protect the client.  Incentive alignment seems off.  Consider dropping this requirement.

If anti-theft is a desirable feature, the best idea I have is a TLS exporter binding.  That's not appreciably more feasible, of course.

comments.author: thibmeu
comments.body:
This is the main reason why the sentence above is

> Origins MAY want to prevent signatures from being spoofed or used multiple times by bad actors and thus require a nonce to be added to the @signature-params.

This is an ask from the origin, as they get benefits. The section probably should be titled "replay detection" rather than "anti-replay" to help carry that framing.

Re-reading, where I believe it reads wrong is that `Agents SHOULD [provide a nonce]` and right after `Clients MUST ensure that this nonce is unique`. This is similar in [section 6.3](https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/draft-meunier-webbotauth-httpsig-protocol-01#name-nonce-validation). It is a confusion as the nonce is always optional for clients, and it's the origin that prompts it.

comments.body:
Just to confirm: are you discussing key format (as in the response that the verifier gets) or the `type`? `type` carries both a format and validation method.

`directory` and `jwks_uri` share the same format already (as you observed in #116, and mentioned in [Section 5.5](https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/draft-meunier-webbotauth-httpsig-protocol-01#section-5.5)): JWKS. As for validation, if we were to keep `jwks_uri` only (as it's more generic), the verifier would have to infer it based on the shape of the URI . comments.body:
I refer to both.  The `type` parameter indicates that the resource has multiple potential formats.  That leads to verifiers having to implement ALL of those formats if they want to be interoperable, which isn't particularly friendly in terms of getting interoperability.  It makes implementation a bigger ask of verifiers.

Not sure what you are saying about what verifiers infer.  That's a separable issue, but the concern I continue to have with "http-message-signatures-directory" (aside from its length, #116) is that it doesn't convey semantics.
```
A: https://example.com/.well-known/jwks.json
B: https://example.com/.well-known/http-message-signatures-directory
```

The first one fetches the JWKS resource, and that's it.
The second one is recognisable as a registered well-known. The verifier can therefore perform a domain binding by validating the directory response accordingly.

The property would therefore be inferred from the URL shape rather than from a specific `type`.

_Note: i agree that having a clearer name for the endpoint could help to be more descriptive_

One point if we remove `type`: that's a breaking change for `Signature-Agent` (we have done that with structured field directory, so it's doable, but worth noting)

issues.author: martinthomson
issues.body:
> To limit tracking risks, implementations SHOULD avoid long-lived, globally unique key identifiers unless strictly necessary. Key rotation SHOULD be supported, and clients SHOULD take care to avoid signing information that could be used to correlate activity across contexts, especially where sensitive user data is involved.

-- https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/draft-meunier-webbotauth-httpsig-protocol-01#section-7.3-1

issues.title: 5.2.1 label-keying MUST vs the Appendix E vectors, and whether 5.2.2 already carries the property
issues.author: AVAVERIFY
issues.body:
Implementing -02 in our merchant-side verifier surfaced a conflict Joshua
Ashcroft's implementer's report also touches (his finding 1): 5.2.1
requires the Signature-Agent member keyed to the signature label to be
covered, but E.1.1 and E.2.1 label the signature sig2 while keying the
member agent2. A strict 5.2.1 reading rejects the document's own vectors.

Two possible fixes, and they differ in reach. Re-keying the vector members
to their signature labels closes the fixture inconsistency. But it may be
worth asking whether 5.2.1's label-matching requirement is itself stronger
than needed: 5.2.2 already requires resolving the member the signature
actually covers, which is the security-relevant property, and matching the
label on top of that adds bookkeeping without adding security. Our verifier
implements the 5.2.2 rule (attribute to the covered member, whatever its
key), passes both the E.2.1 request vector and the E.2.3 directory vector
that way, and we have documented it as a retained deviation from a strict
5.2.1 reading.

Happy to PR either direction once the intended rule is settled.

comments.author: FearmessOp
comments.body:
Data point from another independent implementation (Node.js, @agentsig/core):
we currently apply 5.2.1 strictly, so E.2.1 fails with a label-mismatch error
and we carry it as a negative test. I agree the covered member key is what the
signature actually binds and that label matching on top of it doesn't add a
security property; if the WG settles on the 5.2.2-only reading we'll switch,
and it would let the published vectors stand unchanged. Two implementations
diverging on this seems like a good reason to name the intended rule in -01.

comments.author: AVAVERIFY
comments.body:
One correction to my own text above, since #135 has now reported the same E.2.1 finding and it would be easy to quote the wrong sentence. I wrote that our verifier "passes both the E.2.1 request vector and the E.2.3 directory vector that way." E.2.3 is the signed directory response: a response signature under the label `binding` covering `@authority` and `content-digest`, with no `Signature-Agent` member, so the 5.2.1 keying rule does not apply to it at all. We verify E.2.3, but it says nothing about this question. Only E.2.1 does.

On the substance, #135 adds the option I should have named: renaming the label `sig2` to `agent2` in `Signature-Input` and `Signature` leaves the published base and signature bytes valid, because the label is not in the signature base. That is the smallest change to the vectors. Paired with stating the 5.2.2 rule (attribute to the member the signature actually covers) as the intended one in -01, both implementations here would converge without regenerating anything. The PR offer stands for either direction.

issues.title: §5.2: "expiry" is separated from its antecedent and reads as key expiry
issues.author: pierluc-codes
issues.body:
Against `draft-ietf-webbotauth-httpsig-protocol-00`, §5.2.

§5.2 introduces `expires` as a required `@signature-params` entry, then the
list continues with `keyid` and `tag`, and three sentences on other topics
follow before the recommendation:

> The signing key is available to the agent at request time. Algorithms should
> be registered with IANA as part of HTTP Message Signatures Algorithm
> registry.
>
> The creation of the signature is defined in Section 3.1 of
> [HTTP-MESSAGE-SIGNATURES].
>
> It is RECOMMENDED that expiry be no more than 24 hours.

By that point the nearest concrete noun is "the signing key", and the sentence
says "expiry" rather than naming the parameter. I read it as a bound on key
lifetime.

The document uses that word family for both clocks, which is what makes the
bare noun ambiguous rather than merely loose. §5.5.2 describes a key's own
expiry in the same terms: "Continue to include the old key until its
expiration date", and "Remove expired keys from the directory". The directory
example in §5.5.1 gives such a key a 30-day life (`nbf` 2024-04-11, `exp`
2024-05-11). A reader who attaches the 24-hour figure to keys therefore lands
somewhere the document contradicts by two orders of magnitude, and has no local
cue that they have done so.

In fairness, the paragraph immediately after does resolve it: "A signature
covering @authority alone verifies against any method, path, or body sent to
that authority until it expires [...] expires bounds how long that lasts."
So a reader going straight through recovers one paragraph later. The cost is
that they recover by backtracking, having already formed the wrong reading.
Naming the parameter avoids that for one word.

Suggested fix, either:

- name the parameter: "It is RECOMMENDED that a signature's `expires` be no
  more than 24 hours after its `created`."
- or move the sentence up so it attaches directly to the `expires` entry in the
  `@signature-params` list, where its antecedent is unambiguous.

issues.title: ID Migration
issues.author: sandormajor
issues.body:
I'm thinking how to handle ID migration. E.g. you use the header `Signature-Agent: x="https://bot.example/.well-known/..."` but then the keys move for some reason to `something.example/jwks.json`. If you simply update the header to the new address then all the allowlists/denylists/reputation accrued on the web becomes invalid.

Some components of a solution could be
* Returning a 302 redirect for a period of time when requesting the old json (related: https://github.com/webbotauth/draft-ietf-webbotauth-httpsig-protocol/issues/119)
* Linking the old json from the new one so that verifiers know that it is a successor of the old one
* Co-signing with both keys for a period of time

It becomes more tricky when the migration is not 1:1 but bots split or merge.

A related broader issue here is that the protocol could signify many things (e.g. I'm moving the bot's identity from a.com to b.com) but there is no way to test what the ecosystem does with the signal. During my experiments with WBA it was very hard to even know how websites react to these headers (is the new header going to break a bunch of sites? do they recognize the header? do they parse it correctly? did they adopt https://github.com/webbotauth/draft-ietf-webbotauth-httpsig-protocol/pull/71? if parsing fails, do they fall back to IP verification? do they treat IP and WBA the same way?)
This makes any type of migration very costly.
Maybe something like the [web platform tests](https://web-platform-tests.org/) could help here, but things like "does the reputation carry over" will be very hard to test because providers might not want to share reputation signals back to the client.

comments.author: AVAVERIFY
comments.body:
An implementer's report against the second half of this issue, the part about not being able to tell what verifiers do with the signal, because we can measure a piece of it.

On 2026-09-20 we probed 24 candidate hosts for `/.well-known/http-message-signatures-directory` and found five live directories (bounded probe, not a census: 18 returned 404, one returned 401, three failed DNS). Four serve a JWK Set. One, `www.shopify.com`, serves a bare JWK object with no `keys` member. Two shipped verifiers then give opposite answers on that same directory: the public checker at webbotauth.net rejects it ("Body does not contain a keys array") and will not grade it, while ours accepts it and pins Shopify's exact body in a frozen test. Neither is wrong by the text. Section 5.5.1 says the three types "resolve to a JSON Web Key Set" with no 2119 keyword, and the verifier duty is a SHOULD scoped to entries. So the answer to "do they parse it correctly?" is that the question has no single answer today, and the draft is why. A separate fault on the same host, not to be blurred with the first: the apex `shopify.com` returns a 301 to `www`, and Section 5.5's "MUST be served with a 200" is a real MUST, so a verifier resolving `Signature-Agent: "https://shopify.com"` conformantly gets a discovery failure rather than a key.

Two observations from our own code that bear on the migration question. First, we already branch on draft era on the wire in two places: whether `Signature-Agent` is the legacy bare string or the dictionary form, and whether member resolution is strictly keyed to the signature label or lenient with a fallback. That is a live example of how expensive a signal change already is for a verifier, before any identity moves. Second, each of the three migration components you list (a 302 for a period, the new directory linking the old, co-signing) only helps a verifier that keeps history. Ours keeps an append-only log of (key, domain) observations for exactly that reason: continuity or succession can be computed over the log later, rather than needing a rebuild when the rule arrives. A verifier without such a log sees a migrated identity as a new name, whatever the old directory says about it.

One thing we do not do, since a report that only lists what we got right is not a report: we do not gate the directory response on its media type; a body that parses as a key set is accepted regardless of `Content-Type`. That is on our list.

issues.title: E.2.1: signature label "sig2" does not match Signature-Agent member "agent2"
issues.author: FearmessOp
issues.body:
In Appendix E.2.1 of draft-ietf-webbotauth-httpsig-protocol-00, `Signature-Input` and `Signature` use the label `sig2`, but the `Signature-Agent` field uses the member key `agent2`, and the covered component is `"signature-agent";key="agent2"`.

Section 5.2.1 requires the covered `Signature-Agent` member to be keyed by the signature label, so the example does not follow its own rule.

The signature itself checks out. I re-derived the 375-byte signature base and verified the 64-byte Ed25519 signature against the RFC 9421 B.1.4 public key; both match. This is a naming inconsistency in the example, not a bad vector.

Two ways to fix it:

- Rename the label in `Signature-Input` and `Signature` from `sig2` to `agent2`. The label is not part of the signature base, so the published base and signature bytes stay valid. This is the smaller change.
- Or, if `sig2` is the intended label, rename the `Signature-Agent` member and the `key` parameter to `sig2`, then regenerate the base and signature.

Which one is intended?

Unrelated nit: the draft text still lists https://github.com/thibmeu/http-message-signatures-directory as the source repository; that URL now redirects here.

I ran into this while implementing the profile independently in Node.js (https://www.npmjs.com/package/@agentsig/core), and I'm using the vector as a negative test case for label binding in the meantime.

comments.body:

issues.title: Section 5.5.1: `alg` is restricted to one registry while the container is a JWKS pointing at another
issues.author: kakooch
issues.body:
## Summary

Section 5.5.1 points the directory's `alg` at the HTTP Signature Algorithms registry while declaring the
container a JWKS per RFC 7517, whose `alg` points at the JOSE registry. No value satisfies both. We
probed 75 hosts and the 17 live directories have split three ways, which suggests the sentence is being
read three different ways in the field.

## The sentence

Section 5.5.1, "Directory Format", of draft-ietf-webbotauth-httpsig-protocol-00, in full:

> All three types resolve to a JSON Web Key Set (JWKS) as defined in Section 5 of [JWK]. The alg
> parameter is restricted to algorithms registered in the HTTP Signature Algorithms section of
> [HTTP-MESSAGE-SIGNATURES-IANA].

It carries no RFC 2119 keyword.

## Why the two halves conflict

- The first half makes it an RFC 7517 JWK Set. RFC 7517 section 4.4 says `alg` values "should either be
  registered in the IANA 'JSON Web Signature and Encryption Algorithms' registry established by [JWA]
  or be a value that contains a Collision-Resistant Name", and makes the member OPTIONAL.
- The second half restricts it to the RFC 9421 section 6.2.2 registry, whose six entries are
  `rsa-pss-sha512`, `rsa-v1_5-sha256`, `hmac-sha256`, `ecdsa-p256-sha256`, `ecdsa-p384-sha384` and
  `ed25519`. None of those is in the JOSE registry, and `ed25519` is not a collision-resistant name.

So a directory that satisfies section 5.5.1 violates RFC 7517's guidance on the same member, and vice versa.

A practical consequence: a stock JOSE library parsing the JWKS may reject `"alg":"ed25519"` as an
unknown algorithm, since implementations commonly validate `alg` against the JOSE registry.

## What deployments actually do

One HTTPS GET per host for the well-known path, 75 hosts, September 2026. Of the 17 that served a
directory with at least one key:

| `alg` | hosts |
|---|---|
| absent | 9 |
| `EdDSA` | 7 |
| `ed25519` | 1 |

Data and method: https://github.com/whisper-sec/web-bot-auth-directory-survey

Three observations on that split:

1. The nine that omit `alg` match the document's own examples. No JWK printed anywhere in the document
   carries an `alg` member.
2. The seven publishing `EdDSA` are following RFC 7517's pointer to JOSE. Worth noting that RFC 9864
   (October 2025), which updates RFC 7518, 8037 and 9053, marks `EdDSA` **Deprecated** in the JOSE
   registry and registers the fully-specified `Ed25519` in its place, so that answer has moved.
3. The single `ed25519` is ours, and we arrived at it by reusing one constant for the RFC 9421 signature
   parameter and the JWK rather than by reading that sentence closely. We mention it because it makes the
   sample one-of-one rather than independent corroboration.

Nobody in the sample publishes `Ed25519`. Nothing appears to break in practice, presumably because
verifiers select on `kty` and `crv`, which all 17 get right.

## Suggested resolutions

In order of preference:

1. **Say that `alg` SHOULD be omitted**, and drop the registry restriction. This matches the JWKS
   examples the document already prints, keeps the JWKS a plain RFC 7517 JWKS, and removes the conflict
   rather than picking a side. The algorithm is already fully determined by `kty: OKP` plus `crv: Ed25519`.
2. **Point at JOSE and require the fully-specified value**, i.e. `Ed25519` per RFC 9864, and add it to
   the examples. This keeps the container conformant to RFC 7517 at the cost of a second identifier for
   the same algorithm.
3. **Keep the current pointer but make it explicit**: add an RFC 2119 keyword, note the departure from
   RFC 7517 section 4.4 and why, and put the value in the examples so implementers see it.

Happy to send a PR for whichever direction is preferred.

Context on the measurement: the survey was run against the text as it stood in
draft-meunier-http-message-signatures-directory-05, where the same restriction appeared in section 3.
Section 5.5.1 of the adopted document fixes that sentence's grammar but not the registry question, so
the finding carries over unchanged.

pulls.title: Changes nonce from 32-bit number to string of base64 bytes
pulls.author: EthanHeilman
pulls.body:
This PR changes the nonce from a 32-bit number to a string containing base64 encoded bytes.

My rationale is:

1. Not fixing the size of the nonce enables signers to avoid nonce collisions by selecting the nonce from a larger space.
2. [RFC 9421 HTTP Message Signatures Section-5.1](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9421#section-5.1) allows the verifier to specify in the Accept-Signature header the nonce a signer must use in the signature they generate. Existing code may not assume this nonce is limited to 32-bits.
3. RFC 9421 uses strings of base64 encoded bytes in the examples for nonces so this limitation would be unexpected.
4. It allows for the use of signed or otherwise authenticated nonces such as those generated by a random beacon.

Perhaps we shouldn't limit this to strings of base64 encoded bytes. RFC 9421 defines the nonce as just a string defining it as:

> nonce:  A random unique value generated for this signature as a String value.

What do you think @thibmeu?

reviews.body:
This is a good point! uint32 might be restrictive, and is not needed for the security of the protocol.

reviews.author: sandormajor
reviews.body:
Thanks Thibault!

What I meant on the email thread is a hybrid between the two examples: Using the HTTP Signature-Agent the verifier can tell that the request was indeed signed by directory.test (because it's fetching the JWKS from the .well-known of directory.test), and the data URI Signature-Agent allows to send certificates in the request itself, but the root certificate (for example.com in the example) is self-signed and not tied to example.com in any way.

To make sure that the root key is owned by example.com there needs to be further validation, so I think one solution could be to use a data URI Signature-Agent with only the leaf certificate (sub.example.com in the example) and a pointer to the root/intermediate certificate. I think this could be accomplished with an AIA in the leaf cert, e.g.:
```
X509v3 extensions:
  Authority Information Access: 
    CA Issuers - URI:https://example.com/.well-known/http-message-signatures-directory.crt
```

The verifier would then verify the signature with the public key in the Signature-Agent, match the public key with the leaf cert, then fetch the root cert from the AIA URI and verify the leaf cert with it.

What do you think?

Note that the public key is redundant as it's part of the JWKS and the leaf cert as well, so maybe it's enough to just send that cert when using a data URI header.

comments.author: kandoin
comments.body:
There is an interesting side-effect due to recommending that the key matches the signature label. According to RFC 9421's handling of signature-labels [1], it is allowed by an intermediary proxy to relabel "signature" and "signature-input" headers during transmission and no integrity checks are enforced on the labels.

Now in a scenario where web-bot-auth signatures exists with other http message signatures and if there is a conflict where an existing proxy's behavior chooses to relabel, this will fail the verification and this failure mode will be silent one.

Curious to hear your thoughts on this and see if there are alternative methods to prevent against this edge case (For e.g. including signature-agent as part of the signature params as opposed to a header).

[1] https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9421#name-signature-labels

comments.author: sandormajor
comments.body:
Nice catch, @kandoin! The spec actually says "applications should not rely on specific labels being present, and applications should not put semantic meaning on the labels themselves"

This is interesting because the `Signature` and `Signature-Input` are connected by the label as well. An alternative could be the second example in issue https://github.com/thibmeu/http-message-signatures-directory/issues/70, where a new parameter is added to the `Signature-Input` that points to the `Signature-Agent` like this:
```
Signature-Input: sig1=(... "signature-agent";key="agent1");signature-agent=agent1
Signature-Agent: agent1="https://example.com"
```

comments.body:
Thanks for the catch @kandoin 

Trying to lay out the scenarios below

1. signature-agent;key as a signature-component
If nothing is modified, then all is good
If something is modified, the signature does not validate
I'm under the impression that the proxy could also remove the signature, and then that's not a different threat model

2. signature-agent as a signature parameter
It adds integrity. If an intermediary proxy attempts to modify or tamper the signature, then the receiving server will detect it.
However, if the signature is removed, then it's no different from case 1.
We would have to register a parameter `signature-agent` with IANA in Registry [HTTP Signature Metadata Parameters](https://www.iana.org/assignments/http-message-signature/http-message-signature.xhtml#signature-metadata-parameters)

I'm under the impression that case 1 is sufficient given that with a proxy removing the signature, you end up with a similar result. Getting a signal that the signature has been tampered with may be interesting, but I fail to see how the action from the server of the client would differ

pulls.author: AVAVERIFY
pulls.body:
Closes the request in #120: test vectors for directory signing, valid cases only.

**What this adds.** One new subsection, E.2.4, giving a worked example of the
possession proof on the directory response from Appendix B.1. It shows the fetch
request, the JWK Set response body byte for byte, the resulting `Content-Digest`,
the full signature base, and the `Signature-Input` and `Signature` response
fields. `created` and `expires` are the fixed constants Appendix E already uses,
1735689600 and 4889289600, so the example does not age; a long `expires` is also
what the Directory Response Signature Lifetimes guidance asks for. Ed25519 only.
Issue #11 covers the negative cases, and I have left those alone.

**Key material.** The Ed25519 key from RFC 9421 Appendix B.1.4, the same key
Appendix E already uses, under the same keyid
`poqkLGiymh_W0uP6PZFw-dvez3QJT5SolqXBCW38r0U`. Nothing new is introduced.

**How it was produced and checked.** Every byte is generated, none hand written,
and the two paths do not share code:

1. Generation signs through our Web Bot Auth implementation, so the vector is
   what a running verifier produces.
2. Verification is a standalone script that imports nothing from that
   implementation. It recomputes `Content-Digest` from the body, rebuilds the
   signature base from the covered component list parsed out of the published
   `Signature-Input`, recomputes the JWK thumbprint to select the key, and
   verifies with node crypto. It reads those inputs back out of the rendered
   draft after RFC 8792 unfolding, so what gets verified is what the document
   prints.

Cross checks: the published `kid` equals the thumbprint computed from the key
itself; the same signature does not verify over a modified body; and, as a
control on the key material, re-signing the existing E.2.1 base reproduces its
published signature byte for byte. Generator and verifier live at
https://github.com/AVA-PAY/ava-pay/tree/main/scripts, given only as provenance.

**One caveat, and it matters.** The draft has no worked example for Appendix B.1
today, so this vector necessarily encodes one reading of the normative text:
covered components `("@authority";req "content-digest")` in that order, with
`created`, `expires`, a thumbprint `keyid`, and
`tag="http-message-signatures-directory"`. It carries no `alg` parameter, since
B.1 does not list one. If the working group intends a different construction, say
so and I will regenerate. This is material for the question rather than an answer
to it.

These came out of implementing a merchant side verifier against -01, which is why
the missing example was noticeable.

pulls.title: Separate the possession proof from the domain binding in Appendix B
pulls.author: shivdeep1
pulls.body:
Follows the discussion on #100 and the current list thread on Appendix B scope. Text only, no mechanism change.

## What this fixes

Appendix B holds two properties that behave differently. The **domain binding** is genuinely `directory`-only, because the well-known URI is reserved and an arbitrary path is not. The **possession proof** in B.1 is not: it covers `@authority` and `content-digest` and works on any response that serves key material.

The appendix opens with "It applies to the `directory` type", which is correct for the binding and reads as covering the proof too.

Section 5.5 already draws the distinction this PR carries into the appendix:

> TLS authenticates the host but not the path, and nothing reserves the `jwks_uri` or `cimd` path to the host's operator. The well-known URI is reserved, so `directory` additionally names a domain.

So this is a consistency fix rather than a new proposal.

## Why the reading matters

Under the narrow reading a `jwks_uri` or `cimd` operator cannot produce a conformant proof, since `tag` is pinned to `http-message-signatures-directory`. Two consequences follow:

- 5.5.3 will not attribute redistributed key material to their URL, so the identifier falls back to the thumbprint of 4.3, which does not survive rotation.
- Joshua Ashcroft noted on the list that Cloudflare's documentation instructs signing the directory response with one signature per key. If that artifact is required to enrol, operators on `jwks_uri` cannot produce it. I have not tested whether enrolment rejects an unsigned directory, so that is his report rather than a verified claim.

The second matters more in practice. Wenchong Dong's measurement of 11 August found no origin fetched a published directory across 294,898 signed requests, and concluded that "an allowlist is an enrolment gate under another name". If enrolment is the gate that decides who can usefully sign, an operator who cannot produce the artifact it asks for is excluded structurally rather than by choice.

## Evidence that the broad reading was intended

- #98 (merged 19 June): "We still strongly suggest that jwks_uri response is signed to bound keys to a domain."
- On #100, @thibmeu wrote that a signature over the requested authority "applies both to the delegated and same-origin", and "I would not scope the signing recommendation only to cross-origin/delegated discovery. Would that fit better?" That question was asked in June and picked up this week.
- The -01 changelog records "Move the domain binding to an appendix". The proof travelled with the binding and inherited a scope written for it.

## Implementer reports

Two independent implementers said on the list this week that they apply B.1 to `directory` responses only, because that is what the text licenses: @AVAVERIFY (merchant-side verifier, author of the E.2.3 vectors in #121) and Joshua Ashcroft (two production directories). Neither read it as a design decision.

## Changes

1. Scope paragraph: separate the binding from the proof.
2. Add `{#possession-proof}` so the scope paragraph can reference the section.
3. `tag`: a sentence saying the value names the mechanism rather than the resource type.

## The `tag`

I opened this as the part I was least sure about. RFC 9421 Section 2.3 defines it as "An application-specific tag for the signature as a String value. This value is used by applications to help identify signatures relevant for specific applications or protocols." That ties the tag to the protocol rather than to the resource being served, so one value across response types is the reading that fits rather than a stretch of what `tag` is for. @AVAVERIFY takes the same position below on interop grounds: two values would imply two validation procedures that do not exist. Still your call if you read it differently.

Two further notes. The proof stays **MAY** for non-`directory` types, since 5.5 observes those key sets may serve other consumers and mandating signatures over shared key material would be a real burden. And @AVAVERIFY has offered to extend the E.2.3 vectors to cover the proof on a `jwks_uri` response if the separation is adopted, so the type-generic claim would ship with an executable example on each side.

pulls.body:
Relates to #109 opened by @martinthomson

This moves `Signature-Agent` to only accept a direct JWK Set URI

```
Signature-Agent: agent1="https://alice.example.com/.well-known/http-message-signatures-directory"
Signature-Agent: agent2="https://bob.example.com/.well-known/keys.json"
```

This is a breaking change. It also removes `directory` and `cimd`, which could be added in a future document.

That change seems to have received positive feedback on the list. We should restart a thread though as that's breaking to inform folks.
